title: Paloma and the Will
premise: When the coffin of town founder Edmund Vail is exhumed for a disputed will reading, coroner Hazel Thornbury finds it empty — and discovers the 'dead' witness to Vail's true will may be alive and hiding. As Hazel digs through decades of falsified death certificates, they realize Vail's heirs have been quietly eliminating anyone who knew the fortune was meant for the town's orphanage. Hazel must find the witness — Vail's former nurse, declared dead on paperwork Hazel's own predecessor signed — before the heirs finish the job, ending with Hazel exposing the conspiracy at the will's second reading and choosing to stay in Marrow Creek as the family they built there finally has something worth inheriting.
about_author: Silas Amberdale is the pen name of a former small-town records clerk who spent eleven years filing death certificates in the Appalachian foothills. They write mysteries about the quiet violence hidden in paperwork and the stubborn warmth of towns that refuse to forget their dead.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Establishes Marrow Creek, Hazel's morgue, and their habit of talking to the dead. The court order arrives: exhume Edmund Vail, dead forty years, over a contested will. Emotional beat: unease — Hazel has never opened a grave they didn't close themselves.

chapters.title: An Empty Suit of Clothes
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The exhumation: the coffin holds Vail's suit, a stone, and a 1984 newspaper — but no body. The town erupts. Vail's grandson Charles demands Hazel call it grave robbery and close the case. Beat: dread mixed with the first thrill of a puzzle worth solving.

chapters.title: The Predecessor's Hand
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. In old county archives, Hazel finds the 1984 death certificate for Vail's nurse, Ruth Okafor — signed by Hazel's late predecessor, Dr. Pell. The handwriting doesn't match Pell's other work. Beat: the cold realization the corruption is institutional, not recent.

chapters.title: What the Orphanage Remembers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Dee, a young archivist at the Vail Orphanage who grew up there. Dee recalls Ruth teaching piano before she 'died.' Hazel and Dee form an alliance. Beat: found family begins — two lonely people recognizing each other.

chapters.title: A Brake Line in the Rain
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel's third 'accident' victim is revealed to have been Ruth's accountant. Then Dee's car fails on a mountain road — brakes cut. Dee survives; the warning is unmistakable. Beat: fear curdling into resolve; the stakes turn personal.

chapters.title: The Heirs Apparent
chapters.summary: Charles Vail's POV — the only antagonist chapter. His grief for his grandfather curdles into entitlement; we see him rationalize the falsified death, the bribed doctor, the 'accidents.' Beat: power's corruption shown from inside, almost sympathetic, then not.

chapters.title: Dead on Paper
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Following Pell's old ledgers, Hazel traces a cash payment to a lakeside cabin and finds Ruth Okafor alive, elderly, and terrified — she's been hiding for forty years, keeping the real will. Beat: triumph shadowed by grief for her stolen life.

chapters.title: The Reading of the Will
chapters.summary: Hazel and Ruth's POV, alternating. Charles learns Ruth lives and moves to have Hazel discredited and the evidence seized. Ruth wavers, ready to run again; Hazel convinces her the town is worth standing for. Beat: quiet courage before the storm.

chapters.title: What Edmund Meant
chapters.summary: Climax. At the second reading, Charles produces a forged will leaving everything to the family. Ruth walks in, alive, and Hazel presents the exhumed evidence, Pell's ledgers, and the confession of the dying accountant. Charles breaks; his sister turns on him. Beat: catharsis.

chapters.title: Inheritance
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, weeks later. The fortune funds the orphanage; Ruth plays piano at its reopening; Dee moves into the apartment above Hazel's morgue. Hazel visits Vail's grave — now truly occupied, remains recovered — and finally introduces themself by name. Beat: peace, and a family chosen.
